title: Running a Local LLM on Company Data: What You Actually Need to Know
content_html:
When your team handles confidential client files, financial records or technical specifications, the idea of sending that data to a cloud AI service can feel risky. A local language model on company data sounds like the answer: your documents stay in-house, your AI stays private, and you keep full control. But running a local LLM is not the same as switching on a cloud assistant. It requires real infrastructure, ongoing maintenance, and a clear-eyed view of what you are trading off.

This guide walks you through what a local LLM setup actually demands, when it makes sense, and what to check before you commit.

Why teams consider a local LLM

Privacy and confidentiality are the main reasons. If your business processes sensitive client information, intellectual property or regulated data (like healthcare or financial records), sending that material to a third party's servers, even under a processing agreement, may feel like a risk you do not want to take. A local LLM keeps your documents on your own hardware or your own infrastructure, under your own access controls. That control is real and valuable for teams that need it.

A cloud AI assistant under a processing agreement is perfectly fine for many documents. Contracts, email, meeting notes and routine business writing do not always require local processing. But if your workflow centers on confidential material, a local LLM removes the question altogether.

What a local LLM actually requires

Running a local language model is not free or frictionless. You need three things: suitable hardware, ongoing maintenance, and realistic expectations about model quality.

Hardware. A local LLM runs on a server with a graphics processing unit (GPU). You cannot use an ordinary office computer or your existing server unless it already has one. You need to buy or lease a GPU server, set it up, and keep it running. That hardware costs money upfront and money to operate month after month. Someone on your team or an external supplier needs to manage it.

Maintenance and updates. Once the server is live, it does not maintain itself. The model needs updates, the operating system needs patches, the hardware needs monitoring for failures. If the server goes down, your AI agents stop working. You need either an in-house team with the right skills or a supplier who takes responsibility for keeping it running.

Model quality. The best open-source language models are good, but they are not always as capable as the largest cloud models. They may struggle with nuance, struggle with long documents or give less reliable answers in specialized domains. You need to test whether the model quality is good enough for your actual work before you commit hardware and time to it.

What to check in a local LLM setup

Before you choose a supplier or build one yourself, ask these questions.

Where do your documents live and who can access them? Make sure the setup stores your data only where you want it (on your own server, in your own cloud account, nowhere else). Check that access is controlled by role and permission, not by blanket read access for everyone.

Is every AI action logged? You should see a record of what documents the AI read, what questions it answered, who asked it and when. That log is your audit trail and your safety net.

Who maintains the hardware and the model? If it is an external supplier, what is their uptime commitment and what happens if something breaks? If it is your own team, do they have the skills and the time?

Can you move your setup later? If you decide local AI is not worth the overhead, can you migrate to a cloud assistant or to a different supplier without rebuilding everything from scratch?

When local AI makes sense

A local LLM on company data is worth the complexity if your team regularly processes confidential material and you have the budget and skills (or access to a supplier) to maintain it. If your documents are less sensitive or your team is small, a cloud AI assistant with a processing agreement is simpler and often enough.
